concept.name: Inflation-linked bond
concept.definition: A bond whose principal is adjusted for changes in a price index so that its payments keep pace with inflation. U.S. Treasury Inflation-Protected Securities (TIPS) are marketable securities whose principal is adjusted by changes in the Consumer Price Index; they pay interest every six months and are issued in terms of 5, 10, and 30 years.
concept.intuition: An inflation-linked bond grows your principal with the cost of living, so the fixed coupon you receive is paid on an ever-adjusting, inflation-protected base.
concept.mechanics: The principal accretes (or falls) with the reference price index, and each semiannual coupon equals the fixed rate times the current adjusted principal. At maturity the investor receives the adjusted principal or the original principal, whichever is greater (a deflation floor). The gap between nominal and inflation-linked yields is the market's breakeven inflation rate.
concept.formula: Semiannual interest payment = (fixed coupon rate / 2) x CPI-adjusted principal.
concept.failure_modes: Market prices fall when real yields rise, so TIPS can lose money over periods of rising real rates even as they protect against realized inflation. Index adjustments lag current inflation, and deflation shrinks coupon payments (though the principal floor protects at maturity).
concept.misconceptions: That TIPS cannot lose money — the inflation protection applies to principal at maturity, not to the market price before it. Also, they hedge realized CPI inflation, not any individual's personal cost-of-living increase.
concept.example: A $10,000 TIPS sees CPI rise 3%, adjusting its principal to $10,300; its 1% coupon then pays $103 per year instead of $100.
